title: Urosepsis with Obstructed Kidney: Emergency Drainage and Antimicrobial Pathway

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with sepsis from an obstructed, infected upper urinary tract (usually a ureteric stone) in the emergency department (ED): cultures, antibiotics within 1 hour, urgent imaging, emergency decompression by ureteric stent or percutaneous nephrostomy, intensive care unit (ICU) involvement and delayed definitive stone treatment. Uses the Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand (USANZ) 2025 urosepsis guideline, a 2024 review of European Association of Urology (EAU) and American Urological Association (AUA) stone guidelines, and product information.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-22.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: The Saudi Urological Association urolithiasis guideline (2024) was identified but its text on infected obstruction could not be opened.
USANZ names gentamicin with ampicillin, meropenem, or piperacillin–tazobactam (EAU) but gives no doses; doses are from product information. Gentamicin and ampicillin labels were not opened.
No sourced option for severe (anaphylactic) beta-lactam allergy: discuss with microbiology.
No source gave antibiotic duration or ICU admission criteria.
Typical normal ranges for lactate, white cells and creatinine are not from these sources.
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.

pathophysiology.summary: Urosepsis is sepsis from a urinary tract source and is life-threatening (USANZ urosepsis 2025, Section 1). Sepsis from an infected, obstructed system causes major mortality and morbidity in stone disease (JCM 2024 stone guideline review, Section 4.2). Antibiotics alone do not clear infection behind an obstruction; source control by decompression is needed (USANZ urosepsis 2025, Sections 1.5 and 1.6). Definitive stone removal during sepsis is unsafe and is delayed until sepsis resolves (JCM 2024 stone guideline review, Section 4.2).

symptoms: Loin pain with fever and rigors in a patient with a known or suspected stone (JCM 2024 stone guideline review, Section 4.2).
Feeling very unwell, confusion or reduced urine output as sepsis progresses (USANZ urosepsis 2025, Section 1).
physicalSigns: Renal angle tenderness (JCM 2024 stone guideline review, Section 4.2).
Anuria with bilateral obstruction or a single kidney (JCM 2024 stone guideline review, Section 4.2).
redFlags: Infection with obstruction: urgent decompression, not delayed (USANZ urosepsis 2025, Section 1.5; JCM 2024 stone guideline review, Section 4.2).
Septic shock or organ failure: involve intensive care and infectious diseases (USANZ urosepsis 2025, Section 1.1).
Anuria: urgent decompression (JCM 2024 stone guideline review, Section 4.2).
precipitants: Obstructing ureteric stone (JCM 2024 stone guideline review, Section 4.2).
Other obstruction needing stent, nephrostomy, drain or catheter (USANZ urosepsis 2025, Section 1.6).
Stone procedures, especially percutaneous nephrolithotomy (JCM 2024 stone guideline review, Section 3.5).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: No hydronephrosis or stone on imaging (USANZ urosepsis 2025, Section 1.4).
Collection on CT or ultrasound; percutaneous drainage (USANZ urosepsis 2025, Sections 1.4 and 1.6).
No fever or sepsis; standard stone pathway (JCM 2024 stone guideline review, Section 4.2).

ruleIn.testName: Serum lactate, creatinine and full blood count

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise and culture
actions: Take urine culture and 2 sets of blood cultures before antibiotics (USANZ urosepsis 2025, Section 1.2).
Involve intensive care and infectious diseases when urosepsis is suspected (USANZ urosepsis 2025, Section 1.1).

clinicalManagement.title: Give antibiotics within 1 hour
actions: Give broad-spectrum antibiotics within 60 minutes (see Medicines) (USANZ urosepsis 2025, Section 1.3).
De-escalate once the organism is known (USANZ urosepsis 2025, Section 1.3).

clinicalManagement.title: Image urgently
actions: Get CT or ultrasound to find obstruction, stone, hydronephrosis or abscess (USANZ urosepsis 2025, Section 1.4).

clinicalManagement.title: Decompress urgently
actions: Call urology for ureteric stent or percutaneous nephrostomy; neither is superior (USANZ urosepsis 2025, Sections 1.5 and 1.6; JCM 2024 stone guideline review, Section 4.2).
Send urine collected at decompression for culture (JCM 2024 stone guideline review, Section 4.2).

clinicalManagement.title: Defer stone removal
actions: Plan definitive stone treatment only after sepsis has resolved (JCM 2024 stone guideline review, Section 4.2).

regimens.indication: Empirical treatment of urosepsis with obstruction
regimens.dose: Usual adult dose 3.375 g every 6 hours by 30-minute infusion (indications other than nosocomial pneumonia); 4.5 g every 6 hours is the nosocomial pneumonia dose (Piperacillin–tazobactam label, Sections 2.1 and 2.2).
adjustments: Creatinine clearance 40 mL/min or less or dialysis: reduce per label Table 1 (Piperacillin–tazobactam label, Section 2.3).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Renal function in critically ill patients (Piperacillin–tazobactam label, Section 5).
contraindications: History of allergic reaction to any penicillin, cephalosporin or beta-lactamase inhibitor (Piperacillin–tazobactam label, Section 4).

regimens.indication: Empirical treatment of urosepsis with obstruction and non-severe penicillin allergy
regimens.patientGroup: Adults and children with non-severe penicillin allergy
regimens.dose: Adults: 500 mg or 1 g every 8 hours for complicated urinary tract infection (Meropenem SmPC, Section 4.2). PAEDIATRIC 3 months to 11 years and up to 50 kg: 10 or 20 mg/kg every 8 hours (Meropenem SmPC, Section 4.2).
regimens.route: Intravenous infusion over 15 to 30 minutes or bolus over about 5 minutes
adjustments: Creatinine clearance 26 to 50 mL/min: one unit dose every 12 hours; 10 to 25: half dose every 12 hours; below 10: half dose every 24 hours; give after haemodialysis (Meropenem SmPC, Section 4.2).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Diarrhoea: consider Clostridioides difficile (Meropenem SmPC, Section 4.4).
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to meropenem or any carbapenem (Meropenem SmPC, Section 4.3).
Severe hypersensitivity such as anaphylaxis to penicillins or cephalosporins (Meropenem SmPC, Section 4.3).
Avoid with valproate: levels fall 60% to 100% (Meropenem SmPC, Section 4.4).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Sepsis with a urinary tract source (USANZ urosepsis 2025, Section 1).
Infected obstructed system or anuria from obstruction: stent or percutaneous nephrostomy, neither superior (JCM 2024 stone guideline review, Section 4.2).

teaching.scope: Adults with sepsis from an obstructed, infected upper urinary tract (usually a ureteric stone) in the emergency department (ED): cultures, antibiotics within 1 hour, urgent imaging, emergency decompression by ureteric stent or percutaneous nephrostomy, intensive care unit (ICU) involvement and delayed definitive stone treatment. Uses the Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand (USANZ) 2025 urosepsis guideline, a 2024 review of European Association of Urology (EAU) and American Urological Association (AUA) stone guidelines, and product information.
learningObjectives: Recognise sepsis from an obstructed kidney.
Delay definitive stone treatment until sepsis settles.
pitfalls: Treating with antibiotics alone and waiting.
Attempting definitive stone removal during sepsis.
keyPoints: Fever plus a stone is an emergency.
Stent and nephrostomy work equally well.

patientEducation: Your kidney is blocked and infected; a tube must drain it urgently.
The stone is treated later once the infection has gone.
Return at once for fever, rigors or loin pain if a stent or drain is in place.
lifestyleAndDiet: Drink plenty of fluid after recovery to reduce stone risk.
mdtReferrals: Emergency physician; urologist; interventional radiologist; intensive care; infectious diseases and microbiology (USANZ urosepsis 2025, Section 1.1).
dischargeCriteria: Sepsis resolved, drain or stent working, oral antibiotics guided by cultures, date for definitive stone treatment and stent removal booked.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Urology follow-up for definitive stone treatment after sepsis resolves and for stent or nephrostomy management (JCM 2024 stone guideline review, Section 4.2).
